related_questions.question: What to do if your kid has COVID?
related_questions.snippet: As you would with any respiratory virus, keep your child comfortable with plenty of fluids and over-the-counter pain medication, and monitor their symptoms. If your child isn't eating, drinking, breathing or acting normally, or has a high-risk condition or immunosuppression, please contact your child's care team.

related_questions.question: How long does COVID last in a kid?
related_questions.snippet: How long does COVID last in kids? Most kids get better within one to two weeks. But children who develop complications may need longer to recover. Your pediatrician can tell you more about what to expect.

related_questions.question: How serious is COVID-19 for kids?
related_questions.snippet: Very rarely, COVID-19 can cause death. Some health issues might raise a child's risk of serious illness with COVID-19, such as: Having more than one chronic disease, including those of the heart, lung or nervous system. Not being up to date with COVID-19 vaccination.

text_blocks.snippet: COVID-19 in children is generally milder than in adults, but it can still cause serious illness and even death. The most common symptoms in children are fever and cough, but other symptoms can include sore throat, runny nose, headache, fatigue, shortness of breath, and gastrointestinal issues. While most children recover well, some can develop severe illness or long-term complications.
snippet_highlighted_words: generally milder than in adults, but it can still cause serious illness and even death

list.snippet: Common: Fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, headache, fatigue, shortness of breath.
Severe: In rare cases, children can develop severe illness requiring hospitalization and intensive care.
Long-term complications: Some children experience long-term effects of COVID-19, known as long COVID.
Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C): A rare but serious condition where different body parts become inflamed.
Hospitalization and Death: While less common than in adults, children can still be hospitalized and, in rare cases, die from COVID-19.
Infants: Infants are at higher risk of severe illness compared to older children.
Children with underlying health conditions: Those with asthma, diabetes, obesity, or other chronic conditions are at increased risk for severe disease.
Unvaccinated children: Vaccination significantly reduces the risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death, according to the AAP.

list.title: Vaccination:
list.snippet: Vaccination is the best way to protect children from severe illness and complications.

list.title: Masking:
list.snippet: Masks can help reduce the spread of the virus, especially in crowded indoor settings.

list.title: Social distancing:
list.snippet: Maintaining distance from others, especially those who are sick, can help prevent transmission.

list.title: Hygiene:
list.snippet: Frequent handwashing and covering coughs and sneezes are important.
